speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question which arises out of a telegram, copies of which were sent to the Prime Minister and various other members of the house, in connection with the body blow struck to western Canada by the action of the Canadian Pacific Railway in discontinuing the Dominion, and in closing so many railway stations throughout parts of western Canada.
In view of the representations made by Mr. R. B. Copeland on behalf of the train dispatchers, station agents, operators and telecommunication employees, would the Prime Minister say whether consideration is being given to the establishment of a board of inquiry regarding passenger train operations, which at the same time would deal with all phases of the adverse results which have followed the action already taken?

speakeroldname: Righi Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY
subtopic: PROTESTS OF EMPLOYEES RESPECTING REDUCTION IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: I received a copy of this telegram this morning. I have discussed it with the Minister of Transport, who will be able to reply to the question raised.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY
subtopic: PROTESTS OF EMPLOYEES RESPECTING REDUCTION IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
To answer the second part of the question first, I have been giving some consideration, and so has the government, to the suggestion made by the right hon. gentleman that we might arrange to have the Canadian
Pacific Railway appear before the standing committee on transportation, as I think it is now called, to explain what they are doing and proposing to do in connection with their passenger service, and to allow all interested parties to attend and make representations; in short, to create a forum where these matters can be thoroughly examined.
I confess-and this is not a usual coincidence-that this idea occurred to me two or three days before the right hon. gentleman raised the question. I think it is a very good idea. My colleagues were rather favourably inclined toward it. I spoke to the chairman of the C.P.R. this morning, and C.P.R. representatives would welcome an opportunity to appear before such a committee. I will try, through the usual channels, to arrange for a suitable reference which we could get through the house without prolonged debate so as to get this going once the committees have been set up. The question of passenger service in itself is broad enough and big enough, it seems to me, and if we want to have practical results we should, for the time being, confine ourselves to the whole problem of passenger service and not include other services.
With respect to the closing of stations referred to in the telegram-these, of course, are not on the main line; they are in southern Alberta-I have not had time since receiving the telegram this morning-I have a copy of it too-to go into the matter or even to consult the Board of Transport Commissioners. I should like to do that over the week end and give consideration to what would be appropriate.

maintopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY
subtopic: PROTESTS OF EMPLOYEES RESPECTING REDUCTION IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: I will just say that I appreciate very much the serious consideration given to the proposal I made. If I may reply to the suggestion that three days before I brought it up the minister thought of it, I would point out that I do not have that power of telepathic communication.

maintopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY
subtopic: PROTESTS OF EMPLOYEES RESPECTING REDUCTION IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: I am not sure that the right hon. gentleman's modesty is very becoming.

Canada has cracked back at Russia for accusing this country of supporting a Soviet-alleged revival of German militarism.

Anyone can see he was out on that point by reading the papers this morning.
-but also toward sowing mistrust of the Federal Republic of Germany as a partner in NATO by an entirely unfounded campaign of defamation against it."
The words were the harshest in the foreign policy field to emerge from official Ottawa in a long time.
The harshest words, that is, to come from a spokesman for the department of external affairs. The report goes on:
The spokesman was commenting on a Moscow report Wednesday quoting the Soviet Tass news agency as saying that Canada is supporting the revival of German militarism by permitting West Germany to conduct cold-weather weapons tests at Camp Shilo, Man.
What was the reaction? I can tell the minister there were many people who were concerned about this report, possibly because they had been told nothing about these events in the first place. If they had, they might have been able to put them in a different perspective.
As an example of what happens when people are not told the facts, let me tell the story of one old lady who got in touch with me, quite distressed, to say that our Prime Minister had become an honorary colonel of a German battalion. "I heard the troops shout 'Heil!' when he received the honour." This is what she told me. I made some investigations and found out she had heard this story from Rawhide on his program one morning. This is the sort of thing that happens when the government acts in secret.
What were the reactions to these reports about Camp Shilo? Here is what The Commonwealth had to say on December 22 in an article written by Charles L. Biesick under the heading "Why Are We Training German Troops in Canada?"
They are here! Whether you like it, approve of it or are enraged by it, German troops are training on Canadian soil in preparation for another war.
[Mr. Herridge.l
Aware that they were doing wrong; conscious of their ignoble act against the cause of peace, our government officials wanted this move made in utmost secrecy. They wanted no pictures in the newspapers of the arrival of German troops, tanks and other war machines. They were afraid publicity would arouse too much protest.
Then the article goes on to say:
Let me make it clear my protest against having German troops training in Canada is not prompted by hatred of the German people. I was born and grew up in Canada in a German community. German is the first language I learned at my mother's knee. There is no hate in me for the young German lads who landed at Camp Shilo. They are no doubt as pleasant, nice and clean-cut a group of young men as any of those who dropped bombs on London, Coventry, Warsaw or Stalingrad.
After dealing at great length with this whole question, this writer says:
Had the young Germans been sent to Canada on some peace project, or on a holiday, or to settle here I would have extended them a hearty welcome. But they were sent here by the present powerful military machine in West Germany. They were sent here to complete their training for the same career as their fathers who were responsible for the lives of millions of people in two world wars; including some who went overseas with me.
Then the article deals with the reaction of the Soviet Union. The people of the U.S.S.R., he says, have a reason to fear. To quote further from this article:
T. C. Douglas was a member of the Canadian parliamentary delegation to the U.S.S.R. last summer. At a meeting in Toronto he spoke of the attitude and feeling of the Soviet people. He said: "More than anything, these people have a genuine and deep longing for peace. They are deadly afraid that the Prussian spirit will return to Germany and that Germany will be given nuclear weapons".
The writer goes on to deal with these issues at much greater length, then ends as follows: Being aware that many Germans are opposed to the growing German militarism; being aware that many Germans are actively working and striving for peace and a more decent world, I resent and deplore our Canadian government's being allied with the German militarists against the Germans who are striving for peace.
I resent and protest above all the sneaky, underhanded way the government allowed the Germans and their war machines to be brought into Canada. Yes, as an ordinary Canadian I do ask: What the hell is our government playing at?
The whole article is very well written from the writer's point of view. Then there are the press reports. I have read an extract from the Winnipeg Free Press. Here is something from another paper, a union paper, the Canadian UE News. The article is headed "Protest this madness".

In fact, I have grave doubts that it was and I have a strong suspicion that it was not.

Surely now is the time when we must be concerned about another form of aggression just as important or perhaps more important than military aggression and the enslavement of people, the aggression by countries and by peoples against the civil rights and the civil liberties of humanity. The type of aggression of the Portugals and the South Africas and the Ian Smiths is a very different type of aggression but it is aggression nevertheless against the fundamental human rights of people. The African peoples, Mr. Chairman, are determined to prevent that type of aggression.
It is our part, regardless of the colour of our skin, to join with those peoples in assisting them to carry out their determination. I compliment the government for the very forthright way that it has given support over the last few months to the policies of the government of Great Britain and has supported the resolution of the Security Council of the United Nations seeking the imposition of economic sanctions against Rhodesia. The policies of the government of Canada have resulted, I believe, in effectively preventing trade and commercial intercourse to take place between Rhodesia and Canada.
From time to time the fear has been expressed that, regardless of what action we may take and what action other countries may take, the sanctions against Rhodesia will not be effective because of actions taken by Spain and Portugal. I think there was a fear that Spain and Portugal might be tempted to assist the Smith regime to lessen the effectiveness of the sanctions. I had hoped it would be made clear to Spain, Portugal and South Africa that should they not join with the rest of us in the imposition of sanctions we are prepared to impose sanctions against them also. We must make it clear that we are

February 4, 1966
Supply-External Affairs ready to impose sanctions against those countries that are prepared to assist the Smith regime.
There is some evidence, Mr. Chairman, that the sanctions are becoming effective. The hope has been expressed in the press that within a few months they will be effective. Therefore I think we shall have to look for ways in which we can start conversations and negotiations with those people in Rhodesia who want to establish a legal regime. To this problem, which has been voiced in the public press and in public statements, not very much attention has been paid.
At the Lagos conference the suggestion was made that if the Smith regime were brought down there might be an immediate and temporary period of complete colonial administration. That was one possibility that was voiced. However, it seems to me that we must start exploring ways by which we can start to talk to those people in Rhodesia who want to establish a constitutional and legal regime. I would hope that at some point the minister might deal with that question.
During the course of this debate the opposition has questioned, it seems to me, the propriety and legality of the imposition of sanctions. The questions of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre certainly would seem to indicate the position of his party with regard to the whole policy of sanctions. Surely, Mr. Chairman, there is a general basis and reason for sanctions quite apart from the Rhodesian situation. Heretofore sanctions as a weapon or tool of the international community have been somewhat discredited. I think I am right in saying they have never worked in the past. Certainly, as the hon. member for York South pointed out, they have a very sorry history in the case of Italy. Surely it is up to us in the case of Rhodesia to be determined to see to it that the sanctions work. It seems to me that this matter is one of tremendous importance to the international community. If sanctions do not work, then the only and ultimate weapon, may I say, that the international community has at the moment is force and the use of force.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, it would be terribly significant to the world if we were able to demonstrate to the international community that there is another ultimate weapon that works equally well, namely, economic sanctions. Therefore it is important for us and for all the countries of the world that we should be determined in this instance to see that these sanctions work.

Finally, I should like to say something about the Commonwealth generally. I believe there are in this country a great many people, particularly among my own generation- among the younger generation-who question its validity and value in the world today. May I say that the Commonwealth, it seems to me, serves a very vital and worth-while purpose in the world today. To understand its purpose it is first of all necessary to recognize, as the hon. member for York South did, that today's Commonwealth is very, very different from that of the past and that the new commonwealth, as exhibited at the conference I attended-I hope-is a very different commonwealth.
It is no longer the alliance of Anglo-Saxon oriented white peoples, made up of Britons, Australians, New Zealanders and Canadians. The old commonwealth is very much something of history. Attending the conference in Wellington brought me face to face with this new commonwealth made up of 22 independent nations representing all types and all sorts of peoples, the majority of whom are Afro-Asians. They are people who are rightly proud of their newfound independence and who are rightly determined to fulfil their own national destinies. It is the determination of the black African members to run their own show in their own countries, to develop their own countries for the benefit of their own citizens and to take their place in the community of nations of the world.
I realize this creates great problems. It also, I suggest, presents us with our greatest challenge, the challenge of contemporary race relations. It seems to me that there are few more important factors in international politics today than those raised by the colour of one's skin. If we are to survive, we have to develop ways for all races to co-operate on terms of mutual respect and understanding. We cannot tolerate a world, as we have seen in the past in some instances, with whites sitting in one corner and blacks in another. Yet if we are not extremely careful this is the sort of world that we are going to have. The new commonwealth does serve, I think, the purpose of a trans-racial bridge or link between the white and black races. If we develop our Commonwealth institutions such as the newly developed secretariat and the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association I spoke about a moment ago, I think that the commonwealth will develop as a trans-racial bridge. This is something worthy of all our
February 4, 1966

efforts. May I suggest that Canada has a great role to play in this great commonwealth.
[DOT] (1:10 p.m.)
As the leader of the Canadian delegation to the conference I found that there was a tremendous fund of good will toward Canada and Canadians on the part of the Afro-Asian members. We are trusted and respected. We are not handicapped as Britain sometimes is by coming to the new commonwealth as a former colonial power. Because of Canada's unique position I suggest we must do all we can to strengthen the new commonwealth as a link for good between the various races comprised within its borders. It is essential for the peace of the world, not just for the peace of the Commonwealth, that this approach be established.
I would recall words which Arnold Toynbee wrote shortly before Christmas, and they will bring my remarks to an end:
Modem technology has annihilated distance. It has brought all human beings, all over the face of the earth, into direct contact with each other, for weal or woe.
If we continue to practice the ancient double standard in the atomic age-
He is speaking of the double standard of white and black.
-we are going to destroy ourselves sooner or later-probably soon.
In the atomic age, mankind can survive only if human beings succeed in widening their moral horizon. We have to take the whole human race into the fold of our kith and kin, behaving to all men as we have behaved, in the past only to members of our own minority group.
Our responsibilities-
He is speaking now of the white race.
*-are proportionately great. If the human race were to take the fatal step of dividing on racial lines, a big share of the guilt would be on our heads.

This second session was held in Geneva in 1960 and agreement on this contentious question was almost reached. The Canadian proposal failed to secure agreement by only one vote. This was a great disappointment to Canada because we had taken the initiative in trying to bring some order out of the chaos in international affairs as far as territorial or contiguous fishing zones were concerned.
Then in 1962, as we all know, an election was held. Unhappily some very unfortunate statements were made during that election campaign by the then members of the opposition. I will give no more than one or two examples. Here is one reported by the Montreal Star of April 26, 1962. The present Prime Minister was speaking in Morell, a village in the constituency of Kings.
He told the fishermen of the village that their fishing grounds should be protected by a 12-mile limit and that Canada should set it unilaterally if no international agreement is possible.
In the following year there was another election campaign in the course of which statements even more extreme in character were made. For example, speaking in Sydney in 1963, I believe, the present Prime Minister said:
Now, so far as the 12-mile limit is concerned our purpose is this: as we have not been able to do this by international agreement then we as a Canadian government will declare a 12-mile limit by national action. I think the time has now come

February 4, 1966
Supply-External Affairs
for such action. I am sure that if Norway and Iceland can do this, so can we, and in a way which will not cause difficulties with our friends. I am not afraid of this step-the present government is.
I should like to point out that these statements were somewhat less than trank as an expression of the situation as it was at that time and as it still is. I think the people of the constituencies in which those statements were made realize this and this realization has lowered their opinion of the present government. I think it is not accidental that such constituencies as Gaspe, Kings, Prince, Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare and Halifax, to name a few, voted against the present government on this occasion although they had supported it in the election of 1963.
I should like to place on record the frank statement made by the Prime Minister of New Zealand speaking in the New Zealand parliament on the second reading of a similar bill to the one passed by this parliament in 1964. Here are his words as reported on page 1917 of the New Zealand Hansard:
Right Hon. Keith Holyoake-Questions were asked by Opposition members as to the extent to which any other country could come down here and fish- and members had Japan particularly in mind. They wanted to know to what extent Japan would be bound by this new fishing zone. No country is bound by any definite rule.
[DOT] (1:20 p.m.)
There is no definite international rule because the whole basis of the 12-mile limit was not approved by the international organization.
We have talked about the meeting in Geneva in 1958 and 1960, and I can say that the wider limits have a very solid body of international opinion behind them. The 12-mile zone missed being agreed to by only one vote. As has been said on a number of occasions, a two thirds majority was required-
Later he goes on to say:
Regarding the Japanese attitude, it must be remembered that Japan has never publicly accepted as an exclusive fishing zone any area beyond the 3-mile limit of any country.
As I have said at the beginning, this is a complicated and difficult international problem. The government made a commitment to the Canadian people that it would introduce legislation making a 12-mile fishing zone the law within a year of coming to office. Within that year it introduced legislation which is known as the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act, but the catch was that the government was caught between its extravagant statements on the one hand and the facts of the situation on the other. When it saw itself squeezed between these two situations it adopted the philosophy of the cross-eyed
[Mr. MacLean (Queens) .1
mouse that always saw two cats jumping at him and tried to run between them to get away.
The government introduced a bill which was passed with practically the unanimous approval of the house, I believe, but the catch was that the effective part of the bill, which would cover the fishing boats of nations that had habitually fished near our shores, would not be effective until certain orders in council had been passed. These have not yet been passed. Repeatedly we have asked questions and time and again the government has said negotiations have to be carried out with these other foreign countries which have an interest in the fishing zones that we propose to make exclusively Canadian.
This, of course, is understandable. We have been saying that from the very beginning but the government has been saying that the negotiations were proceeding. It would take an historian to keep track of all the statements that have been made, but back in May, 1964, when the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act was before the house, this was said by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, as found on page 3412 of Hansard:
Both my colleague, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud) and I have already emphasized that we were not in a position to indicate the state of our negotiations concerning our straight base lines and the bodies of water which may be enclosed by these base lines. I am sure this will be understood.
Then he went on:
I am hopeful, however, that our discussions will soon be completed and that the Governor In Council will be in a position before the end of the year-
That was the year 1964 he was talking about.
-to proclaim a list of geographical co-ordinates of points for application of the straight base lines to at least a part of our coast line. If our optimism here proves unwarranted it will not be because this Is not our present appreciation of the situation: it will be because of the nature of the negotiations themselves. It is unlikely that the Governor in Council will publish points covering our entire coast line in his first list.
It is possible that, depending on how our discussions proceed, he will publish several lists and that, in the first, base lines will come into force only for those areas in respect of which we have completed our talks.
This would indicate that there was going to be a series of these orders in council but we have not even had the first one yet.
On September 24 of that year the Minister of Fisheries said in reply to a question, as found in page 8399 of Hansard:
The hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) referred to the order in council passed on the 17th of July exempting certain countries from
February 4, 1966

the application of the 12-mile fishing zone. I am sure hon. members will understand why this was done. It was done for those countries with whom we are negotiating, inasmuch as we could not expect to enforce the 12-mile fishing zone on those countries before the negotiations were completed.
It might be thought that these countries which are exempted from the application of this act would be insignificant countries, not the ones our fishermen have been complaining about for years. But what is the list? I shall quote from the order in council:
The Coastal Fisheries Protection Regulations are amended by adding thereto the following section: 9. (1) Fishing vessels of United States of America are authorized to continue to fish in the fishing zones established by section 4 of the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act.
(2) Fishing vessels of France, Britain, Portugal, Spain, Italy, Norway and Denmark are authorized to continue to fish in the fishing zones of the Atlantic coast of Canada established by section 4 of the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act.
The only important fishing nations that have not been exempted are the U.S.S.R., Poland and Japan. Practically a year went by and still there were no geographical co-ordinates established by order in council. On April 30, 1965, the Minister of Fisheries was asked a question regarding them and he replied, as found on page 779 of Hansard:
On May 6, 1965, as recorded at page 979 of Hansard, the minister was asked a similar question and replied as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I replied to a similar question last week. I wish to assure the hon. member that every possible action is being taken to proceed with the establishment of co-ordinates. However. I should add that the status of negotiations with certain countries makes it advisable to further delay such action as was contemplated in this regard.
On June 11, 1965, the Secretary of State for External Affairs was asked a similar question, which apparently was prefaced with the remark "What are you doing?". He replied, as found on page 2259 of Hansard:
What am I doing, Mr. Speaker? I am working very hard together with my colleague, the Minister of Fisheries, in respect of a negotiation that is proving very difficult.
I do not complain of these negotiations because the establishment of exclusive fishing zones and a straight base line method of measuring are things we all agree should be the objective of Canada as a nation. There is little dissent from that point of view. The only way in which we might differ is as to method.
I think the government has had every co-operation from all parties in the house in its endeavour to bring about such a state of affairs. The ministers have said that if they tell us too much it will jeopardize their
Supply-External Affairs negotiating position and therefore silence in this case is golden and the longer the silence is, the more their hands will be strengthened in these negotiations. It seems to me that the silence has been so long and so deep that their hands should be strengthened to the extent that they could almost demand the whole of the oceans.
[DOT] (1:30 p.m.)
I should like to ask the minister to bring us up to date on the progress being made, if any, in these negotiations preparatory to the establishment of geographic co-ordinates.

I should like to know what is Japan's attitude in respect of this kind of legislation. We have not been told what Japan's attitude has been but we have received some information in an indirect fashion about her attitude to the New Zealand legislation which came into effect on the first day of this year. That legislation was not dependent upon orders in council. I have an article which was published in the Japan Times of December 28, 1965 in which it is stated:
New Zealand issue may be taken to International Court. Japan may lodge an appeal with the International Court of Justice in the Hague against New Zealand's plan to set up an exclusive fishing zone 12 miles off its coasts. The planned exclusive fishing zone is scheduled to go into effect January 1.
A government spokesman said Monday the Foreign Office has sent Masato Fujisaki, Director of the Treaty Bureau, to New Zealand to negotiate on the problem but so far has failed to persuade that country into changing its plan. The government has already decided to bring the matter

Supply-External Affairs before the International Court, if necessary, he said, though efforts would be continued to settle the matter more amicably.

Representatives of the Japanese government stated that they were unable to recognize the validity of the New Zealand zone in terms of its understanding of international law on such questions. Earlier in my remarks I said that at the conference on the law of the sea held at Geneva four conventions were adopted, three in total and a fourth in part. The fourth one not agreed to in total was a convention on territorial sea and contiguous fishing zones.
My understanding is that 27 countries have ratified that convention which has been in effect since September 1964. There was also a convention on the high seas which I believe 35 countries ratified and which has been in effect since September 20, 1962.
There was also a convention on fishing and conservation of the living resources of the high seas. I believe that has been ratified already by 21 countries. It needs one more country to ratify it to make it effective because, as I understand the situation, 22 countries must ratify each convention to make it effective. There was a convention on the continental shelf. Thirty one countries ratified that and it has been in effect since June, 1964.
My question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs is: What is the attitude of the government with regard to Canada's ratification of these four important conventions? I think it is becoming urgent for Canada to ratify these conventions, particularly in view of the fact that Canada took such a leading part in having this meeting called under the auspices of the United Nations.
I should also like to refer to the very important matter of the lack of any international agreement as to what should be the width of territorial waters and/or exclusive fishing zones. It seems to me that the world situation has changed greatly since the last meeting took place in 1960. The attitudes of various countries may have changed. A great many countries have amended or changed their laws in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to speak too long on this first item unless I get carried away a little. But I do feel it necessary to rise in my place and say a few words about the situation in Viet Nam. First, Mr. Chairman, I believe it is important for every member of this house to realize that what is going on in Viet Nam is Canada's business and the business of everyone in this house for several good reasons, because of our dedication to the United Nations, for instance, and for our own protection because we realize that wherever there is a conflict such as there is in Viet Nam there is always the danger of escalation into all-out nuclear conflict which would perhaps mean the end of civilization as we know it.
For those reasons, because of the ideals to which we subscribe, for our own personal protection, because the United States is the acknowledged leader of western policy and our friend and ally and because we are so closely tied to the actions taken by that government, we have a right to examine what the United States is doing in the name
DEBATES	733
Supply-External Affairs of peace and a duty to criticize any action which we think is detrimental to our interests or to the interests of peace and the advancement of democracy in the world generally.
Many members have risen in this house and questioned the legality of the action of the United States in Viet Nam, their right to be there and what they are doing. I think it is long past the time for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to get up in this house and defend or explain the position that the United States is taking. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, the hon. member for York South and myself on earlier occasions have stated that we do not believe that United States intervention in Viet Nam can be defended as legal and that it has no legal right to be there. The United States contends that it is legally there. If our government subscribes to that policy, I believe that to reassure the people of this country who so seriously question this stand the minister should get up and defend the position of the United States or explain why Canada has not protested United States intervention if it is in fact illegal.
People all over the world are worried; their consciences are bothered. As Christians they feel a sense of outrage at the loss of blood in Viet Nam. They feel very uneasy because of the fact that the only explanation given by those who say the United States is right is, "What else are you going to do? Are you going to let the whole of this part of the world go communist?" It is a fact that whatever explanation may have been given from time to time by some people, the only argument heard by the man in the street is that simple statement, "What else are we going to do?" Certainly, Mr. Chairman, that is an argument of despair. That is the best that can be said for it.
Since we subscribe to the ideals of the United Nations and the right of people to have a government of their own choice, I think that the Secretary of State for External Affairs should get up and tell us why he has not dealt with this question, why the United States has not answered the challenge that its intervention in Viet Nam is a deliberate attempt to make sure that those people cannot have the right of choice of a government. To put it another way, do we believe in the right of choice of a government by people only if we are in favour of their form of government?

February 4, 1966
Supply-External Affairs
I suggest that the first indication of how we can judge what the people of that country want is the amount of power that is obtained by those who say they should form the government. It would appear from everything we read that the most powerful forces in that country are those inimicable to the present government which is being supported by the United States. In other words, Mr. Chairman, it would appear that the Viet Cong have the most powerful forces behind them and that if it were not for the United States forces the government of South Viet Nam would have been overthrown and the revolutionary forces would now be in complete control of the country.
We do not judge this, of course, just on the amount of military power that can be raised, but what is most important is the fact that, so far as I at any rate can tell from every reporter who has been on the scene, there seems little doubt that the majority of the population is opposed to the present government now being supported by force of arms by the United States.
There seems little doubt that the most influential people in the revolutionary forces are the communists. I have seen reports that they are more powerful than their numbers would indicate, that there is a relatively small percentage who want to kick out the present government but they are a very powerful percentage. However, I wonder whether we as people who believe in democracy and claim to be Christians can look at the present situation in Viet Nam, realize the kind of slaughter that is going on there and be satisfied in our own conscience with less than a positive opinion that we are backing a government whose actions are legal.
[DOT] (1:50 p.m.)
There are many sources of information on this subject. I recall what may be considered a very unlikely one because it appeared in "True" magazine about a year ago. It is not very often in this house that a member will rise and quote as a source of information a fiction-type man's magazine, but in this magazine an article appeared written by a United States reporter who had been in South Viet Nam for a considerable period of time. He wrote a book-length report on the subject. The important thing is that there was a foreword to his story by Henry Cabot Lodge of the United States. In the foreword Mr. Lodge did not cast any doubt upon the accuracy of the facts stated by the reporter. He did say that the

reporter wrote from a pessimistic point of view and that he was the type of person who would refer to a bottle of whisky as being half empty while Mr. Lodge preferred the point of view that you should talk about it as being half full. This was the only quarrel Mr. Lodge had with the article. Anyone reading the article, and there are others like it, must be impressed by the pure savagery, I could almost say bestiality, of the fighting in Viet Nam. Most of us can recall that in the early stages of the last war there was an outcry against the bombing of Coventry as well as the bombing of other military targets. We asked if it was justified, if it was unchristian, but gradually there was an acceptance of it.
In Viet Nam United States planes and those of the government of South Viet Nam, in trying to fight the revolutionary forces or the Viet Cong as they are called, will hit any village in which they have some reason to believe Viet Cong may be hiding. They hit these villages in such a way as to attempt to destroy every bit of life in them or in the surrounding countryside. The slaughter of the innocent men, women and children is certainly something we can only excuse or go along with in the belief that it is legal or else we can justify it in the same way as we can justify deaths in wartime. These things become necessary to the continued existence of our nation.
However, we are a long way from that in this case. Some arguments may be put forward that this bombing is not completely illegal. So far I have seen nothing to indicate that the position of the United States is even as good as the position of France when France was fighting to hang on in Indochina but was finally forced out. I submit that France at that time at least had the responsibility of a parent nation to a colony to ensure peace, order and good government and to see that there was an acceptable government before clearing out.
I submit that France at least had a colour of right. I suggest it is different in the case of the United States, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs should give us a clear statement whether his government supports the United States being in South Viet Nam at all and whether they support the present methods of the United States since they have advanced from being mere advisers to violent combatants.
I take great exception to the argument put forward by some people, what else are we
February 4, 1966

going to do, just get out and let the communists take over? They say if you let the communists take over there they will take over all of southeast Asia. I take violent exception to the argument for two or three reasons. First, it is no answer to the question. Second, there is no suggestion that the present action is going to prevent the communists from taking over. Third, I believe that this type of action is the greatest assist that can be given to the communists in the worldwide ideological struggle between communists and democracy as we know it.
Certainly I have seen no reports to indicate that the United States, despite the fact they have greatly increased the number of men and the amount of material committed to that struggle, have been able to make any great inroads. The latest reports indicate they are still holding only a few cities and a few strong points and that to all intents and purposes most of the rest of South Viet Nam is under the control of the Viet Cong. The Viet Cong move at will, occupy any position they want and do as they like. The United States forces and the forces of the South Vietnamese government are confined to a few closely held areas and can only make forays in strength into the rest of the country. They are unable to occupy it or hold it.
I can find nothing in the present reports to indicate that the attitude of the people of South Viet Nam has changed or that they are more prepared now to back the present unpopular government than they have been in the past. Human nature being what it is, I find it difficult to believe that the savagery of the fighting and the methods used by the United States in trying to destroy the Viet Cong will endear them to the people of that country. I suggest that the unrelenting determination to kill off the Viet Cong has made it obvious to the people of Viet Nam, indeed to the whole world, that we are careless of how many innocents may die.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that at this stage the war has become a war of terrorism against the people. Since they have not shown any willingness to rise up and get rid of the Viet Cong, the present attitude of the United States seems to be, we will make life so tenuous the people will either want to try to get rid of the Viet Cong or they will have no peace and very little hope of life. I suggest that this is the sort of policy that is going to bother the consciences of the people of Canada generally. At a time when everyone in the country is greatly concerned over the
Supply-External Affairs question of capital punishment and whether or not the state has the right to take the life of a murderer, when we compare our standard of living with conditions that exist in Viet Nam, when we believe the people of other countries have the same right that we have to democracy, then surely we should be doing more than giving mere lip service in regard to this very serious question of the wholesale slaughter of innocent men, women and children in Viet Nam.
It is my contention that were the United States to drop out of South Viet Nam and the Viet Cong to take over, as they likely would, no case has been made out by anyone to indicate that this is going to weaken the western world in its struggle against communism in southeast Asia.
[DOT] (2:00 p.m.)
It seems to have been taken for granted by a lot of the people that the argument will be used: "What else are we going to do? Let them take over?" I submit this argument does not follow logically. In fact, I can only think that since the western case is built on democracy and Christianity, on respect for the rights and lives of individuals, on the right of self-determination, and since we have always made so much of our ideological stand in this regard in the world wide struggle between democracy and communism, every day we do such violence to our ideals in that part of the world we are giving aid and comfort to the communists.
I suggest that the present reaction when we in the western world, who are responsible for the Vietnamese not having free elections to decide their own fate, refuse to recognize their right to self-determination is to send a pang of fear through the heart of every person who wants self-determination in each one of the countries in southeast Asia. There are many parts of the world yet where conditions are ripe for communist infiltration, where there is much poverty and where there is considerable unrest and doubt in the minds of the people about what form of government can best improve their lot in life.
When we continue to say that we have no use for ideals or that we should not be idealistic, we give every person in every one of those countries that we would like to see on our side grave doubts as to our sincerity. I suggest that they have many reservations whether the savagery, the ferocity and the methods used by the communists are as bad as the savagery, ferocity, unfairness and high handedness of the United States in South

February 4, 1966
Supply-External Affairs Viet Nam today when they look at what has happened. It is a case of comparing the theory of the bogey of communism and how bad it can be for them and its actual effects on the United States and the western world with how far we are going to go to save those people from this terrible communist bogeyman. Well might they say, Mr. Chairman, "Lord, protect us from our friends; we will take care of our enemies".
I cannot help but feel that present United States policy in South Viet Nam is the greatest aid and comfort to the spread of communism which exists in the world today. I think the violently anti-communist attitude, as I call it, which says that we should throw away ideals and use any weapons we want and fight in any way we want so as to make sure there will be an anti-communist government in South Viet Nam, is the most tragic and shortsighted policy imaginable. To all intents and purposes the United States seems to have abandoned all hope in the United Nations. Certainly if there were a case for armed intervention, a case to show that the people of South Viet Nam needed armed intervention to protect their rights, then the case should be made before the Security Council of the United Nations. If this task is going to be taken on by the United States instead of by the United Nations, then their right to do so should be defended. Someone should stand up in this house or elsewhere and give the reasons the United States has such a right.
I suggest that when the Secretary of State for External Affairs gives an indication, as he did at page 513 of Hansard, that the government is not entirely in accord with the views or actions of the United States government in South Viet Nam, which is what I read in the last half of the right hand column on that page, then we are entitled to ask in what way it is not in accord. First of all, does the government say that the United States is legally in Viet Nam? Second, does it believe, as the United States apparently believes, that since acting as advisers was not enough and because the Saigon government would be overthrown, the United States had the right to step in with its own force of arms and keep that government from being overthrown?
I need only point out to hon. members that if they look at newspaper reports of a year or two ago they will find that the United States propaganda agencies at that time talked of the South Vietnamese as neutralists and of

the United States as advisers. The insurgents were fighting United States advisers there. In just a year or two the situation has changed. Now the United States is talking as though the Diem government were the real government and saying that it is the government of South Viet Nam which is being supported by the armed forces of the United States against armed intervention from North Viet Nam. Surely, Mr. Chairman, such a metamorphosis in the terms used must show, rather than any basic belief in the rightness of their case, simply a shifting of method and use of terms so that the United States will not have to defend the undefendable.
I think one of the greatest tragedies of the present situation is that is democracies such as Canada and the United States, at a time when such fearful actions are being taken in the name of democracy and Christianity, there should be a complete absence of any logical discussion or argument about the legality or illegality, the rightness or the wrongness, of the situation. I cannot imagine people who believe in democracy so blithely accepting the suggestion that the United States has no territorial ambitions and the proposition that since we are always on the side of right, how can we be wrong? It is a very comforting sort of attitude which they take and a very fearful state of mind, I suggest, for people in any democracy to accept.
I cannot understand how thinking people-and there must be thinking people if democracy in our own country is to remain secure-can accept an argument which is so current and which is, I submit, the only real argument which is heard these days, namely, "Well, what else are we going to do? Let the communists take over?"
I submit that that is the sum total of the argument. I do not want to bore the committee but I repeat that the western world is taking a very fierce attitude. We are acting very savagely. I can find no argument to prove that the United States is in Viet Nam legally. I can find no logic to support the proposition that the Viet Cong will not take over anyway. I can find no argument to dispel my fear that the most logical result of this action is to give aid and comfort to the communists, that it very seriously damages the picture of democracy throughout the world, that it will drive away from us any allies we hope to make, and that it will only give despair to people who believe the great ideology we talk about holds out something for them too.

[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
I hope that the Secretary of State for External Affairs will now put forward to the house and to the people of this country some of the legal arguments that the United States has used to justify its actions. Perhaps some of the arguments, if you look at them, will show that the result of United States actions in South Viet Nam is that they are not doing what they are thought to be doing but rather are helping the communists.

Mr. Chairman, making my first address to the House of Commons after so many outstanding speeches by new members accentuates the awesomeness of the project I now have in hand. However, there is one compensating feature in that I have had the opportunity to appreciate fully the grace, urbanity, acumen and fairness with which the Speaker has conducted the affairs of this chamber. It has also been fully demonstrated that the words I heard voiced during his nomination and election to his demanding and pivotal post were not politely empty words. Mr. Speaker, I extend to you my sincerest congratulations, as I do also to you, Mr. Chairman, and to you, Mr. Deputy Chairman.
Mr. Chairman, yesterday my colleague, the hon. member for Oxford, touched briefly, and my colleague, the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) at greater length, on a subject in which I am greatly interested and in which I believe I have some background of experience. The hon. gentlemen dwelt on the issue of Canadian membership in the Organization of American States, a matter of no little import to our country in the coming years. The hon. member for Oxford held that Canadian membership in the O.A.S. was not desirable and the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) took the opposite point of view. I heartily concur with the former.
At this point, Mr. Chairman, I must crave the indulgence of the house to interject a personal note, and while modesty suggests I abstain the seriousness of the issue dictates that I touch upon it since it may give some added weight to the validity of my observations and conclusions. It was my pleasure, sir, and I consider it my good fortune, to have lived some 35 years in South America in nearly all the countries of that continent. As a young man I slogged across its jungles, deserts and mountains and lived in its small 23033-47
DEBATES	737
Supply-External Affairs towns. Later it fell to me to deal with ministers and heads of state of countries down there.
I have nothing but affection and respect for the peoples and countries of Latin America in their travails and difficulties as they search for a place in the sun. During my years in Latin America I was associated with American interests while retaining my Canadian citizenship. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that Canada enjoys tremendous prestige all over Latin America. We are admired and trusted. The fact, sir, that a large proportion of our population is ethnically French is by no means the least factor engendering those sentiments.
It is of course expressing no new thought to say that Canada has the closest of ties with the United States, both cultural and economic. These ties, eternally I hope and trust, always will be adapted to the maintenance of our basic interests in this close association. Therefore great care, it seems to me, should be taken to avoid burdening those ties and the maintenance and protection of our paramount interests.
I have no doubt that many Canadian individuals as well as officials of our government and members of our diplomatic corps have from time to time had Latin Americans express enthusiasm for Canada's entering the Organization of American States. They have done so in response to a question from the Canadian side as to their attitude on the matter or it has been offered voluntarily.
In the first place, knowing the innate politeness of the Latin, I should not be inclined to accept the response as representing necessarily the result of deep thought or of profound feelings on the matter. In the second place, with all respect to the countries of Latin America, I have a strong feeling that when they think, if they do, upon the question of our entrance into O.A.S. they may equate us only as a permanent ally against what they rightly or wrongly consider to be the colossus of the north. The dissillusionment and the effect on the splendid relationship built up over the years with the countries of South America by Canada, were that preconceived concept to be punctured, would be nothing short of tragic.
Up until the second world war the really great international sport was a game known as twisting the lion's tail. The game continues but it now has a new name: Pulling the eagle's feathers. For good and sufficient reasons I think that our Latin American friends

February 4, 1968
Supply-External Affairs may wish to indulge in this sport. However, I conceive of the relations between Canada and the United States as having progressed beyond this type of proceeeding, which probably would work out to our great embarrassment. Consequently I feel that detachment is in Canada's national interest.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
The O.A.S. is an evolutionary product of the Pan-American union rooted to a degree in the Monroe doctrine. I hope and believe that eventually it will prove a splendid one. However, historically O.A.S. and its predecessor entity have had a long history of discord and difficulties, and our presence now within it might well result in setting back its desirable development rather than promoting it.
If I might be permitted once again to interject a personal note, I can assure hon. members that on many occasions when I lived in South America and when certain conflicts of interest arose between people of the United States and of the host countries I found that by becoming very, very Canadian it was possible to solve some of these really difficult problems. I trust you will not find it unduly presumptuous of me, Mr. Chairman, if I suggest an extrapolation of my small experience into the national scale. For many years in this hemisphere there will be moments when it will be in the paramount interest of Canada to remain silent. Let us not, by being a compulsive joiner, deny ourselves that advantage.
In Latin America the greatest qualities attributed to both France and Britain enjoy what I might call a built-in esteem. Paris and London exert a profound pull. I submit that we here at the northern end of this hemisphere with our dual culture look even more like a bridge than like a cog in a machine.
In the course of my remarks I have emphasized Canada's paramount and vital interests. I make no apology for doing so. As a member of the Canadian House of Commons, if I were to do anything else I should be subverting the position to which the good people of Shel-bourne-Yarmouth-Clare elected me and for which I humbly express my greatest appreciation. Having said this, I feel my position on the issue under discussion is not selfishly Canadian. On the contrary, I believe non-entry into the O.A.S. at this time and perhaps for some years to come is in the best interests of that organization as it is evolving, Latin America, the United States and Canada. I yield to no man in my good will toward

Latin America and the United States. But let us season our good will with a souppon of good sense and a pinch of practicality.

At that time we went to Australia where the conference was being held, and there I found out, by mingling with hundreds of parliamentarians and some Australian citizens, that Canada was held in very high esteem by all.

I decided to take part in the debate because I think that the minister should clear up some points about which many people are in doubt.
As you know, Mr. Chairman, a cultural agreement was signed, on the one hand by the minister of Quebec and on the other, by the minister of France.
That gave rise, from the beginning of 1965 and all through the year, to a controversy on the possible repercussions of that agreement. In my opinion, that matter should be cleared up by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Being myself of Norman descent-my ancestors came from Normandy-it is quite normal for people to think that, along with all my family and colleagues from the province of Quebec, I favour the signing of the most friendly agreement between our former mother country and what we call the mother country of French Canadians in Canada, the province of Quebec.

Mr. Chairman, eight years ago when I first came to the House of Commons I felt myself in almost complete agreement with much that was being done in regard to the external affairs of our country. During those years I have not had occasion to take part in the debates that from time to time have taken place concerning Canada's relations with other nations and the effectiveness of our external affairs policy.
All of us are proud of the reputation Canada has had over the years when becoming one of the more powerful middle powers and all of us have been proud of her role in searching for peaceful solutions to the problems that confront mankind. However, I am a little disturbed at the reluctance of the minister to give us all the information necessary to satisfy ourselves about some of the courses Canada has taken during the past year. I realize some of this information is not as
23033-47J
Supply-External Affairs readily available as people may think and so I do not intend to deal with one or two of the matters that have already been discussed.
But when I look around the world today and see so many emerging nations trying to grasp the fundamentals of democracy, the moral concepts that it stands for, what bothers me is that the image of Canada during the past year cannot but have been tarnished by what has taken place right here within our own borders and right here within the House of Commons. I think of the upheaval in the ministry opposite, the questions that were raised in regard to the conduct of ministers, and the whole question of the administration of justice in Canada.
I also think of the inaction of the Prime Minister, shirking his responsibility to face these problems and calling on Canadians to take part in another election campaign, one that could not help but be destined to result in a parliament not too much different from the one that existed last June. I cannot help but wonder how seriously this has damaged Canada's effectiveness as an example to the emerging nations of the world who are searching and reaching for the fundamentals of democracy. Surely what has happened in this house during the past year has made the problem of those in the Department of External Affairs much more difficult than it might otherwise have been.
Surely anyone who studies history must know that the consequences of these events will follow our foreign affairs officers for almost a generation in their deliberations with other nations. I cannot help but feel that somehow this takes on an even more important significance when one realizes that our Prime Minister was a Nobel peace prize winner. The Secretary of State for External Affairs is his seatmate in this chamber. Surely he must have brought to the attention of the Prime Minister the serious effects that his hesitation and reluctance to deal with these internal matters must have had on nations throughout the world.
I cannot help but wonder what advice the Secretary of State for External Affairs gave the Prime Minister in this regard. I cannot help but wonder, if the Secretary of State for External Affairs had been in the Prime Minister's shoes, whether the situation would have been much different. I cannot help but feel, looking at the effects this will have on the future relations of Canada with emerging nations, that the effectiveness of the Prime

February 4, 1966

Supply-External Affairs Minister as the head of our state has been seriously and desperately impaired. This is something we must face in the days ahead.
The world is perhaps facing the most critical situation it has ever faced. I hope Canada still has some vestige of the good reputation abroad that it had in the past. If it has it should do all that it can to make its efforts for peace more effective, and foster the community of interest between the emerging nations and those that have been established for years.
There are problems within our own borders, and in this connection I speak of the native people of our country. It is only a few years ago since we gave them the vote. I believe it was during the period of time when the Leader of the Opposition, the leader of my party, was the prime minister of Canada.
I have five reservations in my riding and more will have to be done for these native Canadians if we are to fulfil our obligations in this regard and if we wish to have an effective voice in the councils of the world.

I cannot help but wonder what the situation is going to be 20, 30, 40 or 50 years from now. Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief remarks by way of contribution to this very important debate. When I first returned to this house I found the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the position he now occupies and I should like to take this opportunity to compliment the affable and learned gentleman on his attainment of that position. I hope before the debate is concluded we will hear from him about the important policies in respect of several of the situations that have developed.

While he has said he made a full statement to the committee last year, some of us did not have the advantage of being here then to hear him. In addition, a great number of events have taken place since that meeting was held.
Let me first make a plea to the minister to do something for Canadians who serve in his department abroad. I have discussed this matter already with the minister, Mr. Chairman, but I should like to place my remarks on record. One of the wonderful things about being elected a member of parliament is the number of good wishes one receives. I must say that some I received came from employees of the minister's department stationed at various outposts round the world. Almost all of them said: Get back to parliament and get us the vote. I do not understand why in this day and age it should not be possible for the employees of the Department of External Affairs and the Department of Trade and Commerce, as well as other departments, who are stationed abroad to have a say in the affairs of this nation. We have made it possible for servicemen serving abroad to vote in our elections. Admittedly their numbers are larger and are apt to be found in greater concentration where they serve, but this has been made possible for them. Their votes are brought back to Canada and counted.
Perhaps the Secretary of State for External Affairs would consider using his courier service to collect these votes abroad and return them to Canada. It might be necessary to speed up that service during elections or to appoint more people to travel abroad to collect the votes, but I think this could be done. I think to accomplish this is important and necessary. I believe that the fact these people are not able to vote is one of the real sources of dissatisfaction for employees serving in the foreign services. They are permitted to vote when they are in Canada but not when they are abroad.
While I appreciate that on previous occasions during meetings of the External Affairs Committee a statement has been made why it is not feasible to collect these votes and have them counted, my suggestion to the minister is that, over the next two or three months, before the debate on the estimates for the next fiscal year is started, the department draw up the most practical plan it can conceive of to provide an opportunity to foreign services employees to vote. Then perhaps the minister would be good enough to place those
February 4, 1966
recommendations before the committee so that we as parliamentarians could do our best to iron out any difficulties. I am sure that everyone in this committee will agree that this is desirable. All that remains is somehow to bring desirability into practice.
The second point I should like to make deals with the matter of membership, and the wooing that Canada has undergone from certain quarters, in the Organization of American States. In this respect I think that Canadian governments have always come close to seizing the nettle, but at the last moment have somehow refused it as an obnoxious bouquet held out mainly by the international lover, Uncle Sam, and have avoided being drawn into the Organization of American States with the idea perhaps that it is some sort of a harem of the said Uncle Sam. My suggestion is along the lines of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Oxford, that this problem might be solved by more bilateral dealings between this country and Latin America, particularly with Mexico.
The final point I want to make for the consideration of the minister is one that is partially related to his department but has relation to a number of other departments as well. I refer to the International Joint Commission and its activities. Within the next hundred years I believe the hottest political issue that this chamber will face and that future parliamentarians will have to solve will relate to water resources. In this regard I do not wish to go over the excellent speech the hon. member for Kamloops made during the Throne Speech debate. His speech clearly pointed out how valuable water resources are and how important it is to husband and use them properly. That hon. member pointed to the necessity for co-operation of not only a broad range of departments under the control of this parliament and the International Joint Commission but of provincial departments as well. The International Joint Commission and the Department of External Affairs have had a great number of dealings over the years in respect of water problems and policies.
I want to commend to the minister who, if I may say so, is a master of diplomacy with an ability to get along with people-this somehow has not rubbed off on all his colleagues -that he could play a very useful role in developing some statesmanlike long-range approach to our water policy.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to join in this debate today to discuss Rhodesia and I have two reasons for doing so. The first is that we in this party have not hesitated to be critical of the government on many occasions in the past, and on this occasion when we find ourselves in full accord with the government's policy in respect of Rhodesia I do not think we should hesitate to endorse that policy.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
Further, Mr. Chairman, I have had the opportunity of attending the Eleventh General Conference of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association in New Zealand and it has given me a first hand opportunity of assessing the feelings of some of the other member nations of the Commonwealth with regard to the Rhodesian situation. I think there can be very little question that the problem of Rhodesia was on everyone's mind at the Wellington conference. It was an opportunity for me to gauge that opinion and discuss it quite frankly with many of the people who are vitally concerned, particularly the newly emerging and the newly emerged African nations, and recognize how strongly they felt about the entire question of Rhodesia.
For the Commonwealth I think it was a time of crisis. It was a time of crisis because I believe the black nations were waiting to see what the white nations of the Commonwealth intended to do about this matter of Rhodesia which so vitally affected their whole future. They were waiting for an answer to the question, was there going to be a double standard in the Commonwealth or was there going to be one standard? I think it was a time to test the sincerity of the commonwealth, to see whether those words that we always use in relationship to the Commonwealth, namely, the sacred heritage of parliamentary procedure and the great British traditions, were going to be upheld in the matter of Rhodesia. It was a time to prove the value of the Commonwealth and to back up these words with action.
I believe it will be recorded that the Commonwealth may very well have survived because of the action of the United Kingdom, supported by Canada, in the Rhodesian situation. I think we indicated in no uncertain terms that we were willing to back up words with action, that we were willing to recognize the legitimate aspirations of the emerging people in Africa to have a government that



February 4, 1966
Supply-External Affairs would suit them rather than a government that would suit a minority.
I was proud on that particular occasion to be a Canadian. I was proud that Canada took a firm and definite position on sanctions against Rhodesia. I was also proud when later our Prime Minister went to Lagos and helped allay some of the tears that sanctions would not work. I was particularly pleased that he did not wait for everybody else but made a decision and went as a representative of Canada who did not have to wait for everyone else to agree with our country.
To put the question of an embargo in its proper perspective, Mr. Chairman, I think it is important to point out the atmosphere that prevailed in Wellington at the time of the conference. The African leaders were calling for armed intervention and apparently nothing less than armed intervention would satisfy them. Their reasons were that an embargo would be ineffective and that the only test of sincerity from their point of view, the only way they could believe that the white nations of the Commonwealth were willing to support their aspirations, was the willingness of those nations to carry out armed intervention in Rhodesia. They pointed out that in the past, when it was a question of a white minority or a white majority under attack, gunboat diplomacy was practised. They did not feel that the arguments in favour of an embargo were valid for two reasons, first, because it would not work and, second, they believed it was an excuse for not intervening.
It therefore became doubly important to prove both that an embargo could work, could be effective, and the sincerity of our attitude toward the African nations. I believe that by our support of an embargo and the fact that it apparently is working now those fears should be allayed. We have taken this matter very seriously and I think we may be embarking upon something very significant. We may perhaps have found an alternative to bloodshed, because there is very little doubt in my mind that if an embargo had not been invoked, if the situation had been left alone, if merely platitudes had been uttered in place of the action that was called for, bloodshed could very well have occurred in Africa, if not at the present moment certainly later, and it may still occur if the embargo does not prove effective.
I should like to reiterate, Mr. Chairman, that by our action we have probably helped substantially to avoid or put off an African war. I think we have restored the faith of

many of the people of Africa and we may perhaps have proven that there are far more effective ways of creating the rule of law in the world than bloodshed alone. It is a long time since Canada adopted a firm position in foreign affairs, and I believe this image of firmness suits Canada very well. I certainly hope it will continue not only in this area but in other areas.
I should like to say a few things about an embargo or a boycott as it is sometimes called. As I pointed out previously, the Africans were very afraid that this was an excuse for doing nothing. The experience of embargoes in world history has not been the best and certainly has not been such as to evoke confidence. I believe, however, that this time an embargo can work. I think it can work because there are enough people going to make it work.
I can recall that when I was fairly young Italy was bombing Ethiopia and I remember the many occasions upon which world leaders called upon the countries of the world to impose an embargo on Italy. I feel now as I felt then, that had an effective embargo been imposed on Italy we might very well have averted the second world war.
In order for an embargo to be effective we must be prepared for its full consequences, and I was very pleased to hear the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard point out in the debate this morning that if we are going to make this embargo effective it has to be invoked not only against Rhodesia but against any country that helps Rhodesia and tries to subvert the decision of the United Nations in this particular matter.
