I should like to say a few words about the estimates of the Department of External Affairs. I feel we should have an answer to the question raised by the hon. member for Kootenay West this morning when he brought forcibly to the attention of members of parliament the fact that interested organizations such as the Legion, the Canadian Corps and the Voice of Women have deplored the fact German troops were brought into Canada for training. Obviously, the purpose was to provide climatic conditions that were not available in most other countries. It was indicated we were training these troops so that the German army could be used in Russia if necessary.
I believe the Secretary of State for External Affairs is well aware of the fact that the history of the last 15 or 20 years is now history, and that the direction in which the Canadian people have decided they wish to travel as well as the direction in which Russia has decided to travel is considerably different today. If any country should know this, it must be Canada and the Department of External Affairs should be even more aware of it. I believe it is time the Canadian public were informed of the co-operation that is taking place between Canada and the Soviet Union, not that I have much interest in either side of the problem except in terms of what it may mean to the Canadian public.
The other day I had the opportunity of listening to a number of officials from Expo. They were discussing some of the problems they were facing in the development of an international world fair. Some of these problems had never been faced by any nation before, since this will be the largest interna-
Supply-External Affairs tional exposition ever held. Some of the problems were beyond the comprehension of anyone who had been engaged in this type of business before. They were surprised by the fact the Russians were offering them advice and indicating they would supply officials, accounting practices or any kind of help which was needed.
At the same time I was told we were having some difficulty in beating off the overtures of Russia in another field. I refer to shipping in the great lakes and the exporting of our grain. Some Russian ships were helped back into Montreal by a Canadian icebreaker. Following this, it was indicated that these freighters were able to break ice easier than our icebreaker. There have been overtures made to certain officials to provide the Lenin, if we wished, to keep the gulf open for Russian shipping. The reason the freighters waited for the icebreaker, I suppose, was that it did not look right for them to be breaking ice in front of our icebreaker; it would give us a feeling of inferiority. I do not know if they have offered the Lenin, and I am not sure that we want it.
I suggest however that if the Russian people are interested in this field, we in northern Ontario would be quite happy to have the Lenin brought into Hudson bay, so that we would be able to ship grain 12 months of the year from the port of Churchill. It seems to me whether or not this story is true, there is a considerable amount of co-operation between Russia and Canada. I believe this is worthwhile. If it is, then I think it is not fair of the minister or the country to hide behind some stupid protocol, as they do when they scratch the backs of the people of the United States whenever they make decisions. Let us face it, the United States would be very happy if we were to say we would not ship anything to China or Russia. The United States is not able to ship wheat to these countries because of arrangements that were made to protect the merchant shipping of that country. I think our interests do not always parallel the interesis of our allies to the south. We may be developing other allies around the world.
We have much in common with Russia in the area of geography, and the climate in many areas of that nation is not unlike ours. I recall hearing at a reception that one of the problems we were facing in connection with the development of housing in the Arctic had been assisted a great deal by information received from Russia. I refer to the problem of building on permafrost. A year or two

February 4, 1966

Supply-External Affairs afterwards I was surprised to find that the then minister of northern affairs indicated he had been in on these discussions and it was a fact that Russia had indicated to Canada she should scrap her investigations along the lines being followed at the time because Russia had solved the problem of handling permafrost. I did not believe what I had heard earlier; I thought it was just propaganda. The Russians found that the way to handle permafrost was to keep it frozen and refrigeration was the answer. This is something Canadians are now doing.
The only reason I am mentioning this, Mr. Chairman, is that I feel it is time Canadians were told these things and that we try to get along. There is enough opportunity of stirring up differences between the various countries of the world. I think when we are having offers of co-operation from Russia, then the Canadian public should be informed. In my opinion, the Department of External Affairs has more secrets that are not secret than they have secrets that are kept. If I wanted to find out something, and I knew what I was looking for, it would be fairly easy to find it out.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
If Russia is not the great red bear it once was in international affairs as far as Canada is concerned, then why does the government not tell that to the Canadian people? Why do they say they are such terrible people that we must train German troops in Canada so as to provide similar conditions as that found in Russia, and enable NATO eventually to have a force to fight in that kind of climate? The Germans had some experience in this direction during the last war and did not come out of it too well, and I do not think their experience at Churchill will help much either. Last time they played for keeps and lost, and we had better keep it that way. It is not in Canada's interests to do something we do not believe in just because the United States believes it is a nice idea to train these people at Churchill.
I have no objection to extending these facilities to the United States army. We have conducted winter exercises with them at Churchill for some time and our Canadian soldiers are happy about this. Some of the equipment, such as sleeping bags, have been handed on to their poor cousins in the north after the United States army has tested them, and these people have ended up with some nice pieces of equipment.
We should look at this situation from the over-all point of view. I believe Russia is

getting along quite nicely now, but we are taking advantage of them. We are not being honest about them with the Canadian people. If you want the Canadian people to be mad at the Russians, then there are lots of things to bring that about; but they are also doing things which are in our interest.
I do not object to the Lenin steaming up the St. Lawrence to Montreal. When Montreal is faced with an ice jam I think the people of Montreal welcome the Lenin there. I do not know whether anyone said anything about paying for its services, but I believe that this is an icebreaker which can break ice 15-foot thick at 30 knots. If we were able to leave the locks open by use of compressed air, and if we could steam the Lenin up to the lakehead and take on some of the wheat which is waiting there, we could probably solve the problem of boxcars and freight difficulties on the west coast and push this type of friendship a lot further than has been suggested.
Personally I believe Canadians are too timid. I am also aware of the fact that the Secretary of State for External Affairs can draw up the information in such a way that if it is made available to the Canadian public they will not get the gist of it anyway. But the Russians have done a great number of things which are to their credit. They have co-operated with us in Expo to the extent of building the largest pavilion there. They have made offers of technical advice, which I think we will have to take advantage of because it will save us money and which is going to be a factor in the next few months.
Russia has co-operated and been fair with us on a number of occasions in the United Nations and also in the deliberations of the Interparliamentary Union, and if it is true in other fields I suggest that the minister tell the Canadian people. The elections have proved that Canadians are not so stupid that they cannot make some decisions for themselves. In fact, I am always surprised how smart they are. Let the C.B.C. do some programs showing the co-operation we have received, rather than just the bad side of things. We do not have to build our enemies; we make them fast enough without building them; but if there is co-operation, then let us hear about it.
I have another problem which interests me as a Canadian. I am no expert on external affairs and I do not want to be. I have enough trouble with domestic affairs and making my mark there without worrying about external affairs.
February 4, 1966
What concerns me is not the role Canada has to play in Viet Nam, not the sending of troops to Viet Nam, or not telling the United States, rightly or wrongly, whether we will support them. It is the opportunity that we had in 1954 but which we muffed.
I am not opposed to the minister standing up and telling us that this was the fault of the former minister, or the one before him, or the half dozen before him back to 1954. But when Canada had the opportunity of sitting on the International Joint Commission and making available to the world the inspection report which would have indicated who in fact was wrong and should get their knuckles rapped, and how hard, Canada was put in a position of trust, which in my opinion they lived up to for a number of years.
Then in 1964 things changed. The Department of External Affairs found the United States was getting its head beat in, in the role they were playing, so they switched from the report they made the year before and wrote a minority report. In this report they talked only of the atrocities occurring in the north and did not say anything about United States adventures into hard diplomacy with the Viet Cong in South Viet Nam.
It seems to me that if we want to join the United States we should do it openly. But if we want to help them I am not sure that this is the way to do it. The United States is in terrible trouble in Viet Nam, and everyone in the world knows it. If I had the answer to the problem I would write a book, which would probably be a best seller. I do not know what the answer is or what the United States will do, but escalating the war will not solve anything because they are going to get their pants trimmed off. When that day comes then I want to warn Canadians that, rightly or wrongly, Canada will have to support the United Nations. I am not a pacifist, Mr. Chairman, I would join with what was said by the hon. member for Waterloo South. If the day comes when we have to fight, then we will do so, and I will fight.
This situation reminds me of the man who had a brother who drank too much on Saturday nights. His problem was that he always got into trouble. One Saturday night he came home and found his brother, who had had too much to drink again, starting a brawl and getting the hell beat out of him. He did not ask him what started the fight, he just had to help him. He may not have liked it, but that was the situation.

Supply-External Affairs
The same situation applies to Canada, Mr. Chairman. If our role is to be worth while it has to be that of solving the whole problem. That was the role of the international joint commission. It is true Geneva conventions have never been 100 per cent satifactory, but they are made according to world law and are the best we have been able to do.
If the arrangements which were made at that time had been enforced, and if Canada had maintained its impartiality, we would have done the United States a lot more good than by saying to them: "Don't ask us to come out into the open, but in the background we will be all for you until the last drop of our blood is spent". I do not think that sort of thing helps them and it is not what the Canadian public wants.
The Department of External Affairs in Canada is a shame. We are told by the northerners who live above the 49th parallel that they do not get very excited about anything and try to keep everything on a reasonable keel.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
From my limited examination of world affairs nothing is ever that reasonable in international affairs. Nothing is that simple or reasonable. I had the opportunity of attending at the United Nations at one time, and I found that the people who went there would not have anything to do if they were not there, and they would have to go home. Many of them did not go home, and they stayed there and got everything going from one day to another. There were lots of cars, and speeches, and everything that is needed to keep them employed.
It seems to me that the Canadian people are not that kind of people, and that those who represent us are not really representing the average Canadian. We look at things reasonably. We call a spade a spade, and we should do this internationally. Sometimes I call it a shovel, as one of my colleagues says. Perhaps I should say a shovel is a shovel-not that it makes much difference. I do not think that we are trying to relate the issues with what the Canadian people want to do in these matters. I do not think that diplomacy, when it is covered in secrecy, and when you bear all the things in mind that are building up in the external affairs branch, have anything to do with the people. Frankly, we are not big enough to have the kind of external affairs branch that we have. Our role is not big enough. We have built up all the machinery and we have built up the organism, even



February 4. 1966
Supply-External Affairs though we have only the nucleus of an organization to cover it. We have all the protection that everybody else has, and we have not got a big enough external affairs department to do more.
Canada's role, Mr. Chairman, can be a very worth-while one. I think that our role in the world is a very well worth-while one. The external affairs department really is not able, nor is the minister able, with his colleagues, to do anything more than run round the world, doing things that are hardly possible for the Canadian nation. When I say that I am thinking of the role that we have played in some of the other fields that the minister has been involved in, and these are the peace keeping missions. I believe that Canadians have never been guilty, in their service under the United Nations flag, of shooting anybody or starting any calamity in many of these very troublesome situations, and that is so because of the type of people that Canadians are. This has been widely discussed in the United States and elsewhere; and I refer by that to the peace keeping role that could be accomplished both in Rhodesia, if the situation gets worse, and possibly elsewhere. I should like to see Canadian participation in a peace keeping role rather than in an active military role of any nature.
That sort of thing has been talked about very loosely, in my opinion, in the house in the last day or two. We just do not have the kind of soldiers for that. We just do not have the types of members of parliament, and I do not think that Canadians would be prepared to provide men for that.
We have established a reputation, and I am shocked when I see this reputation being destroyed, when it was so hard come by. I am shocked that it was destroyed by the action of the Department of External Affairs. This is not because of the guy that sits on the joint commission in Indochina, or as it is now called, Viet Nam. It is not because those gentlemen have changed their minds. It is because the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and even more than he, the departmental officials he works with, have changed their minds as to the interests of Canada.
I believe we should take a look at what we do, and at the mistakes we made, and at what role we might still play in the joint commission. If this was the interest of the parties that signed the Geneva convention, should we not go back to establishing that boundary, not by war, not by destruction, but by the work

that we originally set up, of which the minister of course is much more aware than I am. But I do think history will indicate that Canada failed when we gave up our active participation, with Poland and India, in trying to make that convention that established the International Joint Commission work, and thus preserve the establishment of the division between North and South Viet Nam.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I do not want to say too much about this, but I do think that is something to which the minister should give serious consideration. That is something that I think many people of Canada and probably many members of parliament believe. It has to do with these dealings and these operations, when they come within the Commonwealth of nations. When we do that we could end up very well.
I have no objection to the decision that was made in Rhodesia. I have no difference of opinion with the decisions made in conjunction with other members of the Commonwealth of nations, of which we are proud to be a member. But I do think if the minister looks at it honestly, and if he asks some of his constituents, but not officials-because they have a role to play-

I rise to speak briefly on one matter which, as it happens, comes directly under vote number one, namely the desirability of Canada's continued participation as a member of the international commission for supervision and control in Indochina.
As a result of various reports with regard to the work of this commission, and particularly as a result of a number of conversations I have had over the last five or six years with personnel who have served in Indochina, I have become increasingly doubtful whether our continued participation in the work of this commission is justified, either on the
February 4, 1966

Supply-External Affairs ground of what is being accomplished-and what there is any possibility of accomplishing in the future-or on the ground of its cost to the country. I think the time has come when a hard look should be taken at this question and a decision reached as to whether we should continue our participation in this commission. If the answer is in the affirmative, we should consider whether we ought to continue it on anything like the scale on which we have been participating in the past.
In my view the present situation makes the value of at least the greater proportion of the Canadian effort in Indochina very questionable. Indeed, most of our people there are able to do practically nothing and their presence is of little value. They are wasting their own time and wasting the country's money by being there in such large numbers.
I would refer to the special report of the international commission dated June 2, 1962 and made, of course, to the co-chairmen in Geneva. The report states on page 10, section 21:
The commission would also like to bring to the notice of the co-chairmen a recent and deliberate tendency on the part of both parties to deny or refuse controls to the commission's terms, thereby completely immobilizing their activities and hindering the commission in the proper discharge of its obligations to supervise the implementation of articles 16 and 17 of the Geneva agreement.
During the last few months there has been a near-complete breakdown so far as this important function of the commission is concerned. The commission considered the situation, and addressed detailed communications to the two parties recommending the resumption of normal controls immediately. (Copies of the letter sent to the two parties are attached as annexure 1 to this report). The commission, however, regrets to inform the co-chairmen that there has been no improvement in this regard.
As far as I am aware there has been no improvement in this regard in the intervening three and a half or four years. These inspection teams are still immobilized. They are unable to carry out their functions. I do not know what purpose is served by maintaining them there. I should like the minister to tell us, when he replies to some of the questions which have been asked, just what activities this commission is carrying on at the present time. Would it not be possible for any valuable work which the commission may still be doing to be done by one tenth or one twentieth of the number of people we are presently maintaining in Indochina? I notice that the cost is reflected in the estimates. As far as the Department of External Affairs is concerned it was $602,000 last year and it is estimated to be $637 000 in the current fiscal

year. It will probably be more than that because the estimate of the previous year was only a little more than half the final expenditure.
The number of personnel listed is 28. But the total number of Canadian military personnel there at the time I was minister of defence-and I do not think the situation has changed since-was considerably more than the number of civilian personnel. The estimates of the Department of National Defence are not set up in such a way as to enable one to isolate the cost of these operations from a military point of view. Nevertheless it is evident that it is considerably greater than the cost listed in respect of the Department of External Affairs. As I say, there are a great many more people involved. I should like the minister to tell us the total cost of maintaining our membership on this commission. It is bound to run between $1,250,000 and $2 million a year. In view of the fact that the commission is not able to carry on the functions it was supposed to discharge, and has not been able to do so for four years or more, I think it is the height of foolishness to be spending this amount of money on maintaining what really amounts to a sham.
It may well be that continued participation by Canada in this commission serves as a convenient screen, excusing the Canadian government from taking any other action. Our continued membership may be justified on this ground to some extent. But I should like to ask this question: If this is the principal purpose our participation serves, is the cost not prohibitive?
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
To sum up, I ask that we get definite information on the total cost, what actual activities these people carry on, whether it would not be desirable to withdraw completely from these activities and, if it is considered that it is desirable we should not, could we reduce the personnel to, at the most, not more than one tenth of the numbers we have had, and possibly one twentieth of those numbers?

The contributions have been most interesting and revealing. One this afternoon by the hon. member for Timiskaming provided the

committee with that feeling that is so necessary from time to time. He has a happy way of speaking and his power of language is only exceeded by the perception of this thought. But as I listen to some of my hon. friends in the N.D.P., who speak with clarity, definiteness and the assurance that their view alone is right, I am not forgetful of the fact that in 1939 the views expressed on September 9 of that year turned out to be far removed from the practical realities of the war that was then just beginning.

I bring to the attention of the minister the fact that within the last year, the power, the prestige and the authority of parliament and our country have been diminished as a result of permitting provinces virtually to enter into treaty arrangements.
When I first brought the matter up it was brushed aside. The amending formula for the constitution is not going to be proceeded with, but tremendous amendments have taken place by arrangement and agreement; by discussions which have weakened the power of the national government and of parliament.
On April 26 last the Secretary of State for External Affairs issued a statement. I am going to read a part of it and I intend to ask him, on the basis of the views that he expressed, how far removed are we today from the authoritative statement which he made at that time. He said:
The constitutional position in this country on the question of treaty-making is clear. Canada has only one international personality in the community of foreign states. There is no doubt that only the government of Canada has the power or authority to enter into treaties with other countries.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill I am presenting to the house provides for the limitation of expenditures and for publicity for federal election expenditures. It proposes to control election expenditures by limiting the expenditures of official agents and of political parties. It also provides that an individual candidate, through an official agent, may spend up to 20 cents for each elector in the constituency. In an average constituency of 50,000 this would mean a limitation of $10,000.
The bill also provides that a recognized political party may spend up to 10 cents for each elector in the constituency in which it has a candidate. As a rough estimate, if a political party ran a candidate in all of the constituencies, this would amount to an expenditure in the neighbourhood of $600,000 to $700,000.
The bill also provides that a sworn statement by the official agents or party officials shall be sent to the Chief Electoral Officer setting out in detail all moneys expended in an election campaign and the names of all contributors to election campaigns.
Subclause 5 of the bill sets out a principle which I feel is a desirable one. It states that any person, corporation, association or trade union is entitled to make contributions to elections campaigns and to political parties. The necessity for this provision arises out of legislation in effect in at least one province, British Columbia, in which there is a limitation placed upon contributions that may be

February 4, 1966
Canada Elections Act
made by a trade union. This is not only in respect of contributions to candidates in provincial elections, as one would have thought, but also applies to federal elections.
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I might :say that the Supreme Court of Canada, as some hon. members will know, by a majority of five to four held that this legislation was valid and within the powers of provincial legislatures in the absence of federal legislation dealing with this matter. I point out to hon. members that if provincial legislatures can restrict trade union contributions to federal election campaigns they can similarly deal with contributions made by corporations or other types of organizations. This could also be implemented by provincial legislation.
I am aware, as I imagine most members of this House of Commons are, that the government has appointed a committee, composed of very distinguished gentlemen, to inquire into this whole matter of election expenses. I was very much interested to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) state that he hoped the committee would be making its report available in April of this year. I am quite certain that report will be of great interest to all members of this house. No doubt it will contain recommendations that will attract the attention of the house, and precipitate legislative steps to deal with this matter.
It is my hope and belief that this report and this matter will be referred to the committee of this house on privileges and elections. Nevertheless, it is my view that there are certain basic principles important to our democracy contained in the bill now before us and in respect of which this parliament is responsible. These things cannot and should not in any way be delegated to a committee made up of individuals outside this house, no matter how experienced or knowledgeable they may be. I doubt if there is any subject upon which all members of this house can claim to have more practical knowledge and experience than the subject of campaign expenditures. This is something with which we are all concerned. Let me say to hon. members that whatever suggestions or proposals may be made by that committee, some of the principles contained in Bill C-5 are essential if we are really to tackle this problem.
The following are the requirements: First, a limitation on campaign contributions; second, publicity in respect to campaign contributions; third, adequate accounting and enforcement of the legislation and fourth, the only way this can be done is by limiting
IMr. Brewin.]
those expenditures to official agents who can account for the funds, and to political parties.
In respect of the second requirement, the need for publicity, information telling where the parties get their money from is far more essential to a genuine democracy than information as to the origination of contributions made to individual candidates. Democracy is something that did not just happen, like an edict suddenly produced. Democracy is the result of design, effort, change and improvement, and required the removal of certain abuses that existed. We in this country of ours, in common with those in the other so-called democracies, have not achieved a perfect or absolute democracy. We still have difficulties and imperfections in our system.
The greatest difficulty in our democracy I suggest is our method of running elections on the basis of large and secret financial contributions from hidden sources not known to the public which is asked to elect representatives. The purposes of this bill are twofold: One, to prevent the buying of political influence by sinister forces in the country and, two, to ensure more fair and independent elections by limiting the amount of brainwashing that can be done by vast expenditures of funds on advertising campaigns designed to sell political parties and political leaders, like soap, to the elector. I believe all those dangers can be dealt with through the provisions of this bill. [DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
That there is a real danger of political influence being bought by secret campaign funds was forcibly demonstrated to this country in the report made by Chief Justice Dorion. Mr. Rivard and his associates were able to get men prominent in the political life of this country to try to exercise their influence on the administration of justice. Why? Chief Justice Dorion makes it abundantly clear. They were able to do that because they had contributed to the funds of a political party. I will not name the political party in the pacific and non-partisan atmosphere that prevails in the house at the present time, but I believe that political party was very much embarrassed by what happened. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) in the election campaign did not fail to call attention on several, and I think repeated, occasions to this matter; but I am not interested in dragging up scandals-although scandal after scandal in Canadian federal history

has been tied up with secret political contributions and until we deal with this cancer on our body politic we will not have an effective, functioning democracy.
We talk about organized crime, Mr. Speaker, but one of the ways to remove the influence of organized crime is to remove the possibility that people like Mr. Rivard can buy influence through the contributions they make to campaign funds. This is one way of dealing with the problem. Anyone familiar with organized crime knows that these syndicates set aside substantial portions of their ill-gotten gains for the purpose of buying influence in political parties. The way to destroy that is by way of publicity, and effective publicity. Does anybody want to see in the published list of contributions, "Mr. Rivard, famous narcotic smuggler wanted in the United States"? I think not, Mr. Speaker.
I have heard it argued that if you have publicity of political contributions it will dry up some of those contributions. Precisely. That is exactly what we want to do, namely dry up some of these contributions. I believe there are enough honest people in this country genuinely interested in political parties, genuinely interested in the welfare of their country, who are indeed willing and not ashamed to have their names associated with the contributions they are ready to make toward running political parties.
I know it is necessary to have money to run our political parties. The particular party to which I belong succeeds in running its campaigns a good deal cheaper, I gather, than some of the other parties represented in the house; but we know, notwithstanding this fact, that there are certain basic and necessary expenditures.
However, Mr. Speaker, why should the people who contribute these funds be ashamed? I think they should in fact receive an income tax deduction to encourage them to do this. I know of no reason why any Canadian citizen should be ashamed to say, "I have contributed to the Liberal party" or the Conservative party, the New Democratic party or the other parties of my hon. friends to my left. I know there is some argument in certain quarters as to whether they are parties, but in my opinion they are certainly parties and are entitled to receive just the same consideration as the rest of us in this and other matters.
I do not think it would benefit the house to enlarge on this matter at great length. The
Canada Elections Act
principle that is involved is fundamental. I challenge the so-called new guard of the Liberal party, and all those Liberal reform elements that we read about sometimes, to make sure that this needed reform is carried out.
I do not suggest for a moment, Mr. Speaker, that this bill contains every useful suggestion in this regard. Many good suggestions have been made, and no doubt will be dealt with by the committee. One suggestion, for example, is that certain basic services in connection with campaigning should be provided free-perhaps certain television and radio time, perhaps one free mailing of campaign literature. Some of these things could well be provided as a free service to bona fide candidates. There are many suggestions of that sort that could usefully be carried out. However, Mr. Speaker, I want to say as clearly as I can that until not only contributions to individual candidates are fully disclosed but the sources of party campaign funds, no real reform will be made and there will be no real dealing with this particular problem.
As we all know, it would be the height of optimism for me to imagine that this house would suddenly at this moment abandon what to my mind is the rather stupid practice of talking out every bill brought before the house by a private member. I am not that much of an optimist that I expect my bill to be passed by the house, even though there are so few of us here, and I am sure all the members who are here are quite intelligent enough to agree with the principle of the bill, and pass it. As I say, I am not that optimistic that this is actually going to happen. This bill will probably be talked out. But I cannot see any good reason why, if the principle means anything to the party forming the government, they should not refer the bill to the committee on privileges and elections. I suspect that this bill will receive the same fate in the house as other private members' bills. But whatever the fate of this particular bill may be, I hope that this parliament-and by "this parliament" I mean this parliament -will see to it that the major and fundamental reform as embodied in the bill is enacted into law during its life.
If we fail to do this, we will be failing democracy; we will be failing to take the opportunity that now lies before us to deal with this problem. The whole of the Dorion report will be wasted if we do not do what I have suggested. That report does not just

not necessary for a man to have access to the expensive public media, to have access to extensive amounts of printed material, to make known to the electors his background and the position of his party.
In those days the electors knew the candidate on a first name basis. These were people who could see him every day of the week. Obviously this time has long since passed. For example, the province in which my constituency and that of the hon. member is will have an average population of about 70,000 people per constituency. Obviously in the period reserved for an election, or even if that period were twice as long, it would be impossible for the candidate to make personal contact with more than a fraction of the people he is to represent. It becomes essential, therefore, for one to use all the written material he can to make known to the electors just what he has done before and what his party proposes to do if and when elected to office.
There are some obvious methods of communication today with which we are all familiar. I refer not only to the party pamphlet but the personal pamphlet which is to be presented on a door to door basis by one's canvassers or sent through the mail to one's electors. All of this costs money. In the large urban type of riding which I and the hon. member represent, this kind of campaigning is perhaps the least expensive of the various modes available.
In recent years, there has been a development for a greater opportunity to make one's merits and one's points of view better known. I refer to such media as radio and television. What is really involved, as I have said, is for a candidate to have a biographical statement prepared for him to be delivered on a door to door basis or through the mail. The objective ot the hon. member is to set a reasonable limit on election expenses. I am saying that expenses in this regard vary tremendously from riding to riding. I put it to the hon. member that the expenses of someone from a small city, such as the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Benson) or the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Faulkner) would, of necessity, be much less because they would have the advantage of being in a centre where all the public media would be focused on them. As the hon. member knows, and as the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) behind him knows very well, in a large metropolitan area with 25 or 30 ridings, it is clearly impossible for a member to have an opportunity of this kind for the presentation of his views, or even to establish his identity as a local candidate.
Now, the hon. member has said that he feels with a limitation on expenses there could be a more intelligent assessment of the candidates and a more intelligent comparison of competing parties. I have a little difficulty reconciling the hon. member's remarks in that regard with the remarks of his leader, or the remarks attributed to his leader, early in the campaign. He was announcing triumphantly that the N.D.P. would have more money to spend this time. I have forgotten how many millions of dollars they were to have, but it was an increase from the election before. Surely, this means that basically the gripe seems to be, not that there is anything wrong with spending money on a campaign, but that at the moment that particular group has not had it. It appears their philosophy would be different if they did.
I do believe it is right that there should be an opportunity for someone to put his views before the public. I feel there are specific ways in which he could be assisted financially. I am sure hon. members are familiar with one of the suggestions in the brochure put out by the committee on election expenses to the effect that there should be free mailing facilities for candidates. Personally, I would endorse that to a limited degree. I agree it could be abused. I agree with the hon. member in his suggestion, and I would be prepared to support legislation which would provide for some part of election expenses being financed by the state. The problem there, of course, is a question of definition, of deciding who is to get a contribution from the state and who is not.

[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
The difficulty, as I see it, for a candidate, a difficulty which could apply, as far as I know, to rural as well as urban ridings-is that a candidate is not engaged in outshouting another, as much as he is engaged in trying to shout his presence into the attention of a society with facilities already geared to engage attention in many other things. Candidates are involved in trying to attract the attention of the electorate at the same time as exponents of sporting events and people talking in other areas of public affairs are seeking that attention; and people engaged in commercial activities are also trying to attract attention. What is necessary for a particular candidate is to be in a position to make such presentation to the public that can be recognized among the din of conflicting claims on their attention by other media.
I think that my principal comment on the hon. member's bill is that I do not think its terms are realistic enough. As far as I know, and I suspect as far as the hon. member for Greenwood knows, he has no real idea whether the limitation would be effective for, for example, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), or whether it would be effective in Port Arthur, or what effect it would have on the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Orange).

That is certainly one of the purposes of the bill.
On the whole I do not disagree with the hon. member's objectives; what I am saying is that the methods used are defective. Other hon. members may have something to say about some of the shortcomings of his proposals, but I would merely point out that the difficulty in which most candidates are involved, as I have said, is that of attracting attention to their candidacy in face of a modern society which is already making great expenditures on advertising, and in which there are other competing interests to attract attention. For this reason I do not feel that the limit imposed by the hon. member in his bill is realistic.
I shall look forward to what the committee on election expenses recommends in this regard. I strongly favour an amendment in the system, not only so that we can have publicity of the kind to which the hon. member referred but also so that we can have, as he has suggested, the benefit of an income tax deduction very much like the charitable deductions which are now available under the Income Tax Act.
In this regard I would not confine the right to deduct necessarily to candidates for federal office. My proposal would be up to $100 a year by way of deductions for any particular individual, and whether the contribution be made to a candidate for federal office, to the central function of a political party, to a candidate for a school board, or for any recognized candidate at any level of government.
Finally, I strongly favour a provision, which I believe is now law in the province of Quebec, whereby some aspect of the expenses incurred by candidates in elections can be paid out of the public purse. However, in the achievement of this I would be concerned that the provision be equitable and that the procedure to be followed, as recommended by the election committee, shall be a practical one and one which really can be carried out.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a bill which purports to bring to Canadian elections what I suppose is a square deal principle. However, as the bill is worded I do not see how it can bring to our election system a square deal unless tremendous changes are made to the bill as it now stands.
If we take the bill at its face value, the proposed section 62A suggests that you be allowed expenditure according to population.
Canada Elections Act
In Yukon Territory, where the population is approximately 20,000, the limit for a party would be $2,000 and the limit for a member himself would be $4,000. Whereas if you were contesting the constituency of York-Scar-borough, where I believe the present population is something like 250,000, the sum of $25,000 would be allowed on behalf of the party and $50,000 to you as candidate. On the face of it, it is ridiculous that one candidate should be allowed to spend $75,000 to get himself elected but another candidate should be reduced to spending not more than $6,000 to be elected.
What are the difficulties involved, Mr. Speaker? The man in Scarborough would probably be relying on mass media-on television programs, radio and the daily papers. It might cost him $500 or more for a program lasting a quarter of an hour. Are we to deny the man who wishes to be elected to the Northwest Territories or to the Yukon mass media of the same proportions? The more I look at this matter the more difficulties I find in the way of this square deal which the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) is doubtless honestly and sincerely attempting to bring about.
I suggest that this is one more encroachment upon the rights of the individual. If we encroach on the rights of individuals to get support from wherever they may find it, to get money in as large an amount as they are able to command, we are not helping individuals but hindering them. Not only that, but we are encroaching on the rights of the people of Canada to support the candidate of their choice or the party of their choice as fervently and generously as they wish.
Although at times a member may be elected to the House of Commons because he represents Imperial Oil and they put $50,000 into his campaign funds, I do not think there are many members in the House of Commons sitting here today who owe their seats in parliament to any one corporation, and in some cases not even to the party which supported them. We have had cabinet ministers, and good cabinet ministers at that, who at times have come down a cropper. Perhaps large sums of money were spent on them in trying to get them elected. I do not think that the amount of money spent in their campaigns necessarily had anything to do at all with whether or not they took their seats in this house.
If we were to put through this bill, even on a unanimous vote, I do not think we would

Canada Elections Act
protect the right of individual members running for parliament, or even the welfare of Canada or the individual rights of the voter himself, the contributor to party funds, by setting an arbitrary limitation on the amount of money he should be allowed to spend on the person or party he wants to support.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I think the right to contribute in any amount should be left to the individual. It might well be that a good man, who is unknown except to a small circle of his friends, might require a large contribution from ten others to give him an opportunity to run. It is passing strange that this objection should come from the corner of the house where they rely on so broad a base to be elected. Is the hon. member for Greenwood so innocent as to think that members of his party have not a decided advantage, if we are trying to level out the rights and privileges of being elected, in being able to partake of what I call saturation campaigning. Without money it is possible to get members of unions, members of unions ten thousand strong, to go up one side of the street and down the other with their representations, and do that with donated time. Is this not a contribution to the party? Is this to be assessed in terms of 10 cents or 20 cents a head?
Am I to think that the hon. member for Greenwood will say that we shall have an independent commission set up to determine how much donated time is worth 10 cents, and how much is worth 20 cents? Because certainly the unions of Canada have been responsible for electing many members of this house by donating their time.
I think that there might be times in my own career where I would have welcomed 10,000 voluntary workers marching about in Athabasca, waving handwritten or perhaps printed pamphlets, ready to shake by the hand the uninitiated or the uninformed and give, as they do, that personal attention which is so necessary to get certain members elected to the house.

Again, in theory it would be very nice to publish the list of those persons who supported any particular candidate. But I think that here we are putting a premium on. dishonesty. A candidate who printed honestly the list of his contributions and where they came from might put his friends on the spot, politically and economically. This would work against him in many cases.
On the other hand a candidate who was not ashamed to sign a false affidavit, who had no respect for the oath and who would not publish such a list, would be in a different position, and his friends and supporters would remain anonymous. I say that he who signed such a true affidavit would be at a disadvantage politically.
I think this is a situation where we could leave well enough alone. I do not think Canada is suffering at the present time by the method in which money for election purposes is raised. If large corporations produce large amounts of money in certain cases, and if the people of Canada are ever alarmed, it is not impossible to raise sufficient money in almost every electoral district in Canada, where the people are alarmed, and where the people want to put forward a man of the people. If the voters of Athabasca got together, and incidentally there are 28,000 people on the voters list, and they each contributed $1, you see what you could get. Incidentally there was nothing like the $28,000 spent. Twenty eight thousand dollars would be only a contribution of $1 per head.
I think my friends are complaining of a situation which does not exist. I am not imputing in these remarks anything improper to certain techniques which I might call saturation campaigning, where certain members enlist thousands of union workers; because that is a very effective way of running a campaign. In my opinion it is more effective than the contributions of large sums of money from any individuals or large corporations.
The technical difficulties are great. Again, if I carry this same line of reasoning into the other arguments, how do you say what is the most valuable? Is it television coverage, or radio coverage, or the use of newspapers or the use of photography? Some members of this house are very photogenic, and their pictures may be reproduced and passed around. This may or may not cost as much as television coverage, or radio coverage, and I merely say this because I could go on making these comparisons until six o'clock.

Therefore I do not think that this bill in its present form will accomplish the purpose for which it is designed. If you ever get to the point where hon. members can ever sort out all of their problems, and arrive at a value to be based on political campaigning, then this bill would be as thick as the Canada Elections Act itself.
If this bill purported to cut out some of the other anomalies and inadequacies of our electoral act, I should support it with a full heart. However there is one thing that I might say: What about the rules regarding elections in the armed forces? If the hon. member for Greenwood will sponsor a bill to reform that act, then I will support it with a full heart. I think that you could drive a four-horse team through that act. Certainly without very much imagination it would be possible to find out exactly how every member of the armed forces voted. Secrecy of the ballot is a fundamental right, but how every member of the armed forces voted could be found out. It would not cost the nation anything to reform that part of our electoral act. We should give to the members of the armed forces the right to secrecy of ballot which is enjoyed by every citizen of Canada.

Yes, but it illustrates the difficulties of this plan. I might have to take affidavits myself-affidavits relating to travel, cost of meals and so on. Would the hon. member accept the affidavits I produce to show that money spent, say, on hiring halls, was actually paid out? Some of these difficulties might be removed if a government commission were set up to run an election from A to Z. Any time on the air would be paid for by a government official. Then what would hon. gentlemen on my left say? They would say the whole election was being run by the minions of the treasury bench. They would certainly not trust these people to run their campaigns for them. Neither would I.
So, I say again, leave well enough alone. Our election system, by and large, is adequate. We have a democratic right to support the candidate of our choice with as much money as we feel we should give. I do not believe the average member here is brought into his place by the expenditure of money. Indeed thousands of dollars were spent in my constituency to see that I was not returned. I welcomed it because the people of my constituency were sickened by the wanton spending of money, the source of which was unknown to them. One reason I am here, one of the lesser reasons, is because a money campaign does not always pay off. On the other hand, I do not see why I should disclose the name of every constituent of mine who sees fit to put his dollar into the plate to

maintopic: CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LIMITATION OF ELECTION EXPENSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not believe there are many members of this house who would not agree with the principle of this bill. One thing it .does is to take cognizance of the very high .cost of campaigning, a cost which has grown over the past few elections.
While we can agree that something ought to be done in regard to this matter, we should also take into account the fact that a committee has been set up to do this very job. I hope the committee will be able to report to this house before too long in order to provide hon. members with an opportunity to study its findings and recommendations.
I am sure most reasonable members of parliament who view these things objectively would agree that the conduct of politics and public affairs should not be placed in the same category as selling soap or automobiles, where campaigns are effectively based on repetition and simplicity. This is the whole concept of good advertising in these fields. Unfortunately there seems to be a high degree of effectiveness in "selling" candidates at election time along these same lines. As far as I am concerned, speaking from my own experience, we in this group do not seem to have as much money to spend on election campaigns as either one or the other of the so-called old fine parties. In some areas within the range of mass media we find there are very important differences in support because of repetition over television and radio and in "the newspapers. I hope something can be done about it.
I agree with the contention of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), the sponsor of this bill, that it is important we should try to do something to remove the opportunity for buying influence during election campaigns. Mr Justice Dorion drew attention to this problem in his report. Many of us know it is not confined to the personalities of whom he was speaking.
However, there are some weaknesses in the bill. There is much talk about limiting the amount of the contribution which can be made by a company, a union or other organization. Surely if this is to be effective there should be some way by which the whole amount, equivalent to 10 cents or 20 cents per elector, could not be paid by one organization. Any organization putting up the whole amount would certainly be in the position of

the man who pays the piper: It would expect to call the tune. A candidate who had been elected after a campaign in which the whole of his expenses had been paid by a single organization, whether a corporation or a union, or by a single individual, would certainly be beholden for his support.
The bill talks about limiting the expenses of a party. Yet our election system does not recognize parties at all. As far as I know there are no papers handled by the chief electoral officer which identify parties.
Surely, this house must pass Bill No. C-85 sponsored by my hon. friend from Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson), to allow for the inclusion of the entity known as a party under the Canada Elections Act, before we could give effect to what the present bill says in at least one of its clauses.
I agree, and this party agrees, that something ought to be done about this problem. We take cognizance of the fact that some progress has been made by setting up a committee to study the situation. I hope this committee will recommend some kind of legislation which will achieve at least some of the objectives which the mover of the present bill has in mind.
